references.implementationNoticeBody: The browser-side results in this demo are measured from the browser's Temporal implementation (native Temporal / temporal-polyfill) and its time-zone and calendar data. They may differ from the specification depending on the browser or version.

ixdtf.title: IXDTF and RFC 9557
ixdtf.body: IXDTF is the RFC 9557 format that adds bracketed annotations such as time-zone names and calendars to RFC 3339 date-time strings. It carries not only an instant, but also information about how that value should be interpreted and displayed.

temporalApi.title: The TC39 Temporal API
temporalApi.body: Temporal is the ECMAScript date-time API being standardized by TC39 to replace Date. It provides immutable types such as Instant, PlainDate, and ZonedDateTime, and treats time zones and calendars as explicit values.

temporalIxdtf.title: Temporal's string format and RFC 9557
temporalIxdtf.body: The string format Temporal reads and writes is based on RFC 9557 (IXDTF). ZonedDateTime.toString() emits an IXDTF string with a time-zone annotation — plus a u-ca annotation for calendars other than ISO 8601 — and ZonedDateTime.from() parses the same format.

goParsing.title: Parse and Validate in Go ixdtf
goParsing.body: Parse returns the date-time and extension information. Validate checks the format and extensions without returning a value. This demo's validate-only mode maps to Validate and shows library error messages verbatim.

temporalParsing.title: Parsing IXDTF with Temporal
temporalParsing.body: Strings with a time-zone annotation are parsed by Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from. RFC 3339 forms without that annotation fall back to Temporal.Instant.from. By default, Temporal rejects a conflict between the numeric offset and time zone.

offsetConsistency.title: Offset and time-zone consistency
offsetConsistency.body: In IXDTF, the numeric offset and time-zone annotation can disagree about the instant. Go ixdtf's strict mode makes this an error; non-strict mode leaves an elective annotation unapplied and preserves the original offset. Temporal rejects the conflict by default.

roundtrip.title: Parse → Format round trips
roundtrip.body: A round trip parses a string into structured date-time data and then formats it back into a string. Even when the instant is preserved, omitted precision, annotation handling, or normalization can keep the output from exactly matching the input. This page compares Temporal and Go ixdtf on the same aspects.

dstAmbiguity.title: DST overlap and offsets
dstAmbiguity.body: When clocks move back at the end of daylight saving time, the same local time occurs twice. An IANA time-zone name alone leaves the instant ambiguous, but IXDTF can make it exact by carrying the applicable UTC offset too. Temporal uses a valid input offset to resolve which occurrence was meant.

zoneArithmetic.title: Time-zone annotations and calendar arithmetic
zoneArithmetic.body: ZonedDateTime's add({ days: 1 }) is calendar arithmetic that preserves the wall clock, while add({ hours: 24 }) is exact-time arithmetic. Across a DST boundary the day is 25 hours long, so they diverge. Because IXDTF carries the IANA time-zone name, the distinction can still be computed after deserialization.

calendarAnnotation.title: The u-ca calendar annotation
calendarAnnotation.body: The u-ca tag carries which calendar the same instant should be interpreted and displayed in. Temporal recomputes era, year, month, and day via withCalendar; Go ixdtf carries the tag without interpreting it. The instant itself (unix_nano) is unchanged by the tag.

suffixSyntax.title: IXDTF suffix syntax
suffixSyntax.body: After the RFC 3339 portion, IXDTF can append a time-zone annotation [Area/Location] and key-value extension tags [key=value]. u-ca is the Unicode calendar annotation. RFC 9557's ABNF defines their order and allowed characters.

criticalAnnotations.title: Critical annotations (!)
criticalAnnotations.body: An ! immediately after the opening bracket tells a recipient not to act on the whole string unless it can process that annotation. An elective annotation without ! may be ignored when an implementation does not understand it.

rejectedExtensions.title: Experimental and unsupported extensions
rejectedExtensions.body: Keys beginning with an underscore are for experiments in controlled environments and must be rejected in normal interchange. Go ixdtf also rejects x- private extensions. Interop exposes these implementation differences as learning material.

about.title: IXDTF & Temporal
about.tagline: The new JavaScript date-time API and the IETF string format that carries its values — what each is, and how they relate

ixdtf.heading: IXDTF — a data-format standard (RFC 9557)
ixdtf.body1: IXDTF (Internet Extended Date/Time Format) is a data-format standard published as RFC 9557 in April 2024 by the IETF SEDATE working group. It extends RFC 3339 — the internet-standard timestamp format — in a backward-compatible way, allowing bracketed annotations (a suffix) after the date-time.
ixdtf.body2: Annotations include an IANA time-zone name such as [Asia/Tokyo] and key=value extension tags such as [u-ca=japanese]. An annotation prefixed with ! is critical: an implementation that cannot understand it must treat the whole string as erroneous. A value can thus carry not only "which instant" but also the machine-readable context of how that instant should be interpreted and displayed.
ixdtf.exampleCaption: Anatomy of an IXDTF string: an RFC 3339 date-time + a time-zone annotation + a calendar annotation

temporal.heading: Temporal — the ECMAScript date-time API
temporal.body1: Temporal is the new JavaScript date-time API being standardized by TC39 (the ECMAScript committee). Designed to replace the long-standing shortcomings of Date (mutable values, no time-zone support, zero-based months, and more), it provides purpose-built immutable types such as Instant, PlainDate, and ZonedDateTime.
temporal.body2: The centerpiece, Temporal.ZonedDateTime, holds an instant + an IANA time zone + a calendar system as a single value. That is what makes calendar arithmetic across DST transitions and projection into calendars such as the Japanese one work correctly. On browsers with a native implementation (Chrome 144+ / Edge 144+ / Firefox 139+) this demo uses that Temporal directly; on other browsers it reproduces the same API with <polyfillLink>temporal-polyfill</polyfillLink> (by fullcalendar). The Playground and Interop screens show both side by side, with the implementation name in each result label.

relation.heading: How they relate — an API and its interchange format
relation.body1: Serializing a Temporal.ZonedDateTime as text needs information that RFC 3339 alone cannot carry — the IANA time-zone name and the calendar. TC39 worked with the IETF to standardize this serialization format, and it became RFC 9557 (IXDTF). The bracketed time-zone notation follows what Java's java.time had long used de facto; RFC 9557 made it an open standard for the first time.
relation.body2: In Temporal, ZonedDateTime.toString() produces an IXDTF string and ZonedDateTime.from() parses one. With the format now an open standard, implementations outside JavaScript — the Go ixdtf library in this demo — read and write the same strings, so IXDTF works as an interchange format between implementations.
relation.body3: RFC 9557 deliberately leaves the consumption of annotations to each implementation's discretion, and Temporal applies its own profile (rejecting unknown critical tags, its own handling of x- / _ extensions, and so on). The same string may be accepted by one implementation and rejected by another — you can watch this happen on the Interop and Guide pages.
relation.diagramCaption: Both implementations read and write the same IXDTF string — the theme of this whole demo

dstOverlap.title: DST overlap
dstOverlap.body: On the night daylight saving time ends in Los Angeles, the wall clock reaches 01:30 twice. Compare two IXDTF strings with the same date, time, and zone name by their numeric offsets and the instants resolved by Temporal.
dstOverlap.parseError: Temporal could not parse this IXDTF string
dstOverlap.conclusion: The bracketed time-zone name carries the region's rules, while the numeric offset pins the local time to an exact instant. Although both read 01:30, -07:00 and -08:00 identify instants one hour apart.

zoneArithmetic.title: +1 day vs +24 hours
zoneArithmetic.body: Add "one day" and "24 hours" to 01:30 on the night DST ends. That day is 25 hours long, so calendar arithmetic and exact-time arithmetic land on different instants. Because IXDTF carries the time-zone annotation, the distinction still computes correctly after deserialization.
zoneArithmetic.goParsed: unix_nano from Go ixdtf strict parse
zoneArithmetic.conclusion: +1 day keeps the 01:30 wall clock and advances 25 real hours; +24 hours keeps real time and the wall clock becomes 00:30. Go ixdtf strict-parses the IXDTF strings Temporal produced and reaches the same instants — IXDTF works as the interchange format between implementations.

calendarProjection.title: u-ca calendar projection
calendarProjection.body: The u-ca tag carries which calendar humans should read the same instant in. Temporal interprets the tag and recomputes era, year, month, and day; Go ixdtf carries it losslessly without interpreting. The instant (unix_nano) never changes.
calendarProjection.projectionError: Could not project into this calendar
calendarProjection.conclusion: epochNanoseconds is identical across every projection. The annotation changes how the instant is read, never the instant itself.

guide.title: RFC 9557 learning guide
guide.tagline: Learn what IXDTF adds on top of RFC 3339

rfc3339.heading: Differences from RFC 3339
rfc3339.body: RFC 3339 specifies date, time, and UTC offset. RFC 9557 (IXDTF) extends it with bracketed annotations appended afterward, so extra information such as the time-zone name and calendar system can travel with the value in a machine-readable form.

suffix.heading: Suffix syntax
suffix.body: An optional [Area/Location] time-zone annotation comes first, followed by zero or more [key=value] extension tags. u-ca denotes the calendar system, e.g. [u-ca=japanese].

critical.heading: Critical flag (!)
critical.body: Prefixing an annotation with ! marks it critical. A parser that does not understand a critical annotation must reject the whole string. Unknown non-critical annotations may be ignored.

rejected.heading: Rejected cases
rejected.body: Private extensions starting with x- and experimental extensions starting with _ are rejected by ixdtf. In strict mode an offset that disagrees with the time zone is also rejected. These are worthwhile pitfalls to experience.

samples.basicRfc3339: Basic RFC 3339 form. IXDTF is a superset of RFC 3339.
samples.basicUtc: Z denotes a time in UTC. RFC 9557 redefines Z as 'local offset unknown' (equivalent to -00:00), distinct from +00:00.
samples.unknownLocalOffset: -00:00 is specified to mean 'local offset unknown' and is distinct from +00:00.
samples.fractional: Fractional seconds (nanosecond precision) combined with a time-zone annotation.
samples.timezone: With an [Asia/Tokyo] time-zone annotation that agrees with the offset.
samples.dstOverlapEarlier: The first 01:30 before DST ends. Offset -07:00 selects the earlier instant.
samples.dstOverlapLater: The second 01:30 after DST ends. Offset -08:00 selects the instant one hour later.
samples.offsetMismatchLenient: Offset (+02:00) disagrees with the zone. Lenient: ixdtf accepts, Temporal rejects.
samples.calendarJapanese: [u-ca=japanese] selects the Japanese calendar. The instant is unchanged; only the rendering differs.
samples.calendarHebrewRfc: An example from the RFC 9557 text, selecting the Hebrew calendar.
samples.timezoneCritical: Critical time-zone annotation [!Asia/Tokyo]. Parsers that cannot honor it must reject the string.
samples.criticalUnknownTag: An unknown tag marked critical [!foo=bar]. Non-strict ixdtf accepts and records it as critical; Temporal rejects.
samples.unknownTag: An unknown but non-critical tag [foo=bar]. Both implementations accept it (ixdtf keeps the tag; Temporal ignores it).
samples.privateExt: An x- private extension. ixdtf rejects; Temporal ignores and accepts.
samples.experimentalExt: A _ experimental extension. ixdtf rejects; Temporal ignores and accepts.
samples.offsetMismatchStrict: Offset mismatch under strict mode. Both implementations reject.
samples.garbage: A string that cannot be parsed as a date-time. Both implementations fail.

why.heading: Why this demo exists
why.body: RFC 9557 (IXDTF) is a modern format that carries time-zone and calendar annotations alongside a date-time in a machine-readable way. This demo round-trips the same string through two independent implementations — Go's ixdtf library and the browser's Temporal API (native or temporal-polyfill) — so you can understand the format and its interoperability hands-on. It runs with no ads and no tracking.
